title: The widow's two mites (Mark 12:18–44)
hook: the great commandment, then a widow gives everything she has

segments.voice: Yesterday, image: the coin carries Caesar's face, and every person carries God's image. Your line was you bear his image. Today, still in the Temple, two tiny coins.

The collection basket comes down the row at Mass. Some people drop in an envelope. Some tap their phone. A kid puts in a quarter his mom handed him. Nobody's watching, or so you hope. Today, somebody is. Jesus is still in the Temple, still being questioned. Then the questions stop, and he sits down across from the treasury, where people drop their offerings into the collection chests, and watches. Rich people put in large amounts. Then a poor widow walks up with two tiny coins.
screen: `THE COLLECTION BASKET.` → `HE SITS AND WATCHES.` → `A WIDOW WITH TWO TINY COINS.`

segments.voice: First, the greatest commandment. A scribe asks which commandment is first of all. Jesus answers with the Shema, words Jews still pray today. In the Douay-Rheims: "Hear, O Israel: the Lord thy God is one God." Love him with your whole heart, soul, mind and strength. And the second: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." The scribe agrees, and Jesus tells him: "Thou art not far from the kingdom of God." In Mark, a warm moment between Jesus and a scribe. Second, a warning. Right after, Jesus warns about scribes who love long robes and the best seats, and who devour the houses of widows. Third, the widow. She drops in "two mites, which make a farthing." Mites were lepta, tiny copper coins. Jesus calls his disciples over: "this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury." The rich gave from what they had left over. She, out of her want, "cast in all she had, even her whole living." Fourth, two ways to hear it. The traditional reading hears praise: whole-heart love, the commandment lived out with two coins. Some readers also hear a lament, since the story sits right after the warning about those who devour widows' houses: a system that takes a poor woman's last coins. The two readings can stand together: the widow is honored, and those who would take from her are warned. Either way, Jesus measures her gift by what it cost her, not by the amount.
screen: `THE SHEMA: LOVE WITH YOUR WHOLE HEART.` · `BEWARE THOSE WHO DEVOUR WIDOWS' HOUSES.` · `TWO MITES, MORE THAN ALL.` · `MEASURED BY COST, NOT AMOUNT.` · then, large: `SHE OF HER WANT CAST IN ALL SHE HAD.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself what a two-coin gift would be for you today: not a big donation, something small you'd actually feel, like your lunch hour for someone who needs to talk, the last of the good coffee, a few dollars you were saving, an apology that costs your pride. Pick one, picture giving it, and notice the little pinch. If you pray, you can offer it to God.
Mites. Two tiny copper coins, lepta in Greek, that a poor widow dropped into the treasury: more, Jesus said, than all the rich gave. Today's word.
Your line: all she had. Two coins, and Jesus called it more than all the rest. Day two hundred twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Catholics give at the offertory of the Mass and through almsgiving, one of the three traditional practices of Lent alongside prayer and fasting, and the Church teaches special care for widows and the poor.

chat.says: How could the widow's two tiny coins be worth more than the rich gifts?
options: The rich gave from extra; she gave all she had. Jesus measured the cost.
Old coins like hers were rare, so they were worth more than gold ones.
Her coins were for the poor, while the rich gifts paid for buildings.

notes: Douay-Rheims Mark 12:29, 12:31, 12:34, 12:42–44 given from memory; confirm wording.
The Sadducees' question (12:18–27) is not retold, only the section's second half; confirm acceptable.
The 'lament' reading (e.g. Addison Wright, 1982) is presented as what 'some readers also hear', beside the traditional praise reading; confirm balance.
Lepta as the smallest coins in circulation; two lepta = one quadrans ('farthing'): confirm.
The Shema is described as prayed by faithful Jews 'then and now': a neighbor reference only, not comparative.
